negatives.text: The operator $P_{\mathcal{F}} f = f_\mathcal{F}$ is the orthogonal projection of $f$ onto the subspace of $\mathcal{F}$-measurable functions in $L^2(\mu)$.
The conditional integral $\int f d\mu$ given a sub-$\sigma$-algebra $\mathcal{G}$ is a $\mathcal{G}$-measurable function $g$ such that $\int_A f d\mu = \int_A g d\mu$ for all $A \in \mathcal{G}$.
If $ \mu $ and $ \nu $ are product measures, then the measure of $ A \times B $ is $ \mu(A)\nu(B) $.

anchor_text: If $ V/U \cong W $ via a linear map induced by the quotient map, then $ U = \ker(\pi) $ and the dual space $ W^* $ injects into $ V^* $.
positive_text: If $ M/N \cong L $ via a module homomorphism induced by the quotient map, then $ N = \ker(\pi) $ and the dual $ L^* $ injects into $ M^* $.

negatives.text: A polynomial function on a finitely generated free module can be seen as an element of the symmetric component of its module homomorphism tensor algebra.

anchor_text: Let $f: A \to B$ be any morphism in the category of sets. The image of $f$ is the smallest subobject of $B$ through which $f$ factors, and the induced morphism from $A$ to the image is an epimorphism.
positive_text: Let $f: A \to B$ be any function. The image of $f$ is the quotient of $A$ under the equivalence relation $x \sim y$ if and only if $f(x) = f(y)$.

The pullback of two inclusion maps $ A \hookrightarrow X $, $ B \hookrightarrow Y $ is the product $ A \times B $ when $ X $ and $ Y $ are disjoint.

anchor_text: If $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ is a sequence of measurable functions on a product measure space with independent projections, then any tail measurable set has measure 0 or 1.
positive_text: For a sequence of independent random variables $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$, any tail event is trivial, i.e., its probability is either 0 or 1.

negatives.text: If $ \mathbb{E}[X] $ exists and is finite, then $ \frac{1}{n} \sum_{k=1}^n X_k \to \mathbb{E}[X] $ almost surely for i.i.d.\ $ X_k $.

anchor_text: A function $ f : A \to B $ is uniquely determined by the subset $ \{ (x, f(x)) : x \in A \} \subseteq A \times B $.
positive_text: A morphism $ f : A \to B $ in the category of sets is uniquely determined by the image of the canonical graph morphism from the terminal cone.

negatives.text: A monomorphism $ f: A \to B $ is a split monomorphism if there exists a morphism $ s: B \to A $ such that $ f \circ s = \mathrm{id}_A $.

anchor_text: A function $f: A \to B$ is surjective if for all $b \in B$, there exists $a \in A$ such that $f(a) = b$.

anchor_text: A linear map from a finite-dimensional vector space to another is surjective if and only if its dual map is injective and maps the dual of the codomain to the dual of the domain.
positive_text: A homomorphism between finitely generated free modules is surjective if and only if its dual induces an injective map on the dual of the codomain.

anchor_text: A finitely generated module is semisimple if and only if it can be expressed as a direct sum of simple submodules.

negatives.text: A linear operator $ f: V \to V $ over a field $ \mathbb{F} $ is nilpotent if and only if some power of $ f $ maps all vectors to zero.

negatives.text: A matrix $ L $, with row sum zero and positive off-diagonal entries, encodes a connected structure if and only if the dimension of the subspace of vectors $ x $ satisfying $ Lx = 0 $ with no vanishing component sum is zero.
The shortest recurrent interaction pattern in a matrix is identifiable via the first nonzero trace in a sequence of its powers.
There exists a decomposition of the adjacency matrix as a sum of rank 1 symmetric matrices with non-zero entries only corresponding to cliques.

anchor_text: A morphism from a terminal object $ 1 $ to an object $ S $ in $ \mathbf{Set} $ corresponds to selecting an element of $ S $.
positive_text: A function from a singleton set to another set $ S $ picks out a unique element of $ S $.

negatives.text: For any set $ X $, the function set $ X^Y $ is defined as the set of all functions from $ Y $ to $ X $, and evaluation is a function $ \text{eval}: X^Y \times Y \to X $.

The image of a function $f: X \to Y$ is the collection of values $f(x)$, and if $f$ arises from a quotient by an equivalence relation on $X$, then the image is the set of equivalence classes under $f$.
If $f: A \to B$ and $g: B \to A$ satisfy $f \circ g = 1_B$, then $f$ is surjective and $g$ is injective.

anchor_text: If $ X_n $ is a martingale with $ \sup_n E[|X_n|^p] < \infty $ for some $ p > 1 $, then $ X_n $ converges in $ L^p $ and almost surely to a limiting random variable.
positive_text: Let $ f_n $ be a martingale with $ \sup_n \|f_n\|_p < \infty $ for some $ p > 1 $. Then $ f_n \to f $ almost everywhere and in $ L^p $.

negatives.text: For a nonnegative measurable function $f$, the integral $\int f d\mu$ is equal to $\int_0^\infty \mu(\{x \mid f(x) > t\}) dt$.
For a non-decreasing sequence of non-negative measurable functions $ f_n \uparrow f $, we have $ \int f \, d\mu = \lim \int f_n \, d\mu $.
If $\nu$ is absolutely continuous with respect to $\mu$, then there exists a measurable function $f$ such that $\nu = f \cdot \mu$.

anchor_text: A function on a group is central if it is constant on conjugacy classes.
positive_text: A function on a group is central if its Fourier transform is diagonal in the irreducible representations.

negatives.text: The space of functions on a homogeneous space admits a Fourier decomposition indexed by irreducible representations.

For a unitary irreducible representation $ \rho $, let $ \phi_{ij} $ denote its matrix coefficient; then $ \int_G \overline{\phi_{ij}(g)} \phi_{kl}(g) \, dg = \delta_{il} \delta_{jk} / d $, where $ d $ is the size of the matrix.
Averaging a function over a compact group under its own Fourier transform maps it onto its zero-frequency component.

anchor_text: A skew Schur function is invariant under the involution $ \omega $ if and only if its conjugate shape is the same.
positive_text: A generating function for skew tableaux is invariant under transposition if and only if the conjugate shape is the same.

negatives.text: The number of tensorized tableaux that commute is equal to the number of pairings under which row column insertions cancel under symmetric content restriction.
A shape-scaled tableau is a semistandard tableau where column vector contents are normalized by the tableau shape’s row counts.
Transpose-invariant Young tableaux generate Schur functions that are transposition invariant under reversal of row indices.

anchor_text: Let $ M $ be a finitely generated torsion module over $ \mathbb{Z}[x] $, and let $ f $ be multiplication by $ x $. If the annihilator of $ M $ is generated by $ x^r $, then there exists a chain $ m_1, \dots, m_r $ such that $ f m_1 = 0 $, $ f m_2 = m_1 $, $ \dots $, $ f m_r = m_{r-1} $.
positive_text: Let $ V $ be a finite-dimensional vector space over $ \mathbb{R} $, and $ \phi \in \text{End}(V) $. If $ \phi $ has zero as an eigenvalue of multiplicity $ r $, then there exists a sequence $ v_1, \dots, v_r $ with $ \phi v_1 = 0, \phi v_2 = v_1, \dots, \phi v_r = v_{r-1} $.

negatives.text: The kernel of a linear map is the set of all vectors that map to the zero vector.

Let $ V, W $ be vector spaces over $ F $. The annihilator of the image of the linear map $ V^* \times W^* \to (V \otimes W)^* $ given by evaluation is the set of functionals that vanish on all simple tensors $ v \otimes w $.
Let $ V \xrightarrow{T} W $ be a linear map over a field $ \mathbb{F} $. The preannihilator of $ \mathrm{im}\, T \subseteq W $ is $ \ker T^* \subseteq W^* $.

anchor_text: The number of closed walks of length $ n $ from vertex $ i $ to itself in a graph is equal to $ (A^n)_{ii} $.
positive_text: The $ i $-th diagonal entry of the $ n $-th power of the adjacency matrix corresponds to the count of $ n $-length loops rooted at vertex $ i $.

negatives.text: If a vector in $\mathbb{R}^n$ is partitioned into cluster segments with rapid variation in magnitude at segment boundaries, then it aligns with the eigenspace of a block-structured matrix.
Two symmetric matrices are spectrally matched if they share the same multiset of eigenvalues and their orthogonal projectors onto eigenspaces are unitarily equivalent.
A column in a matrix is said to be reducible to other columns if it lies in the cone spanned by those other columns.

anchor_text: The number of standard Young tableaux of shape $ \lambda $ equals the count of bijective labelings of the Young diagram $ \lambda $ under row-strict monotonicity.
positive_text: The coefficient $ f^\lambda $ of the Schur function $ s_\lambda $ in the monomial symmetric function $ m_{1^n} $ counts the number of standard Young tableaux of shape $ \lambda $.

negatives.text: The Schur function has an axial decomposition reflecting the number of axial semistandard Young tableaux with bounded content differences.
The skew Schur function $ s_{\lambda / \mu} $ is zero if $ \mu $ is not contained within $ \lambda $, or if the set difference does not form a horizontal strip.
The symmetric function encoding of a sequence of Young diagrams is equivalent to a Schur generating function derived from Fomin’s growth diagrams.

anchor_text: Let $ f(z) $ be a rational function with a pole at the radius of convergence. The number of reachable states at step $ n $ corresponds to the coefficient of $ z^n $ in the Puiseux expansion.
positive_text: The number of reachable states in a finite automaton with $ n $ letters per step and bounded memory follows a rational recurrence.

negatives.text: The number of $ K_r $-free and $ K_s $-free graphs grows sub-exponentially and the growth is best approximated by an exponential generating function with logarithmic corrections at leading order.
Let $a_n$ be the number of permutations of $n$ elements with an even number of cycles; then $ \sum a_n \frac{x^n}{n!} = \cosh(\log \frac{1}{1 - x}) $.

The number of permutations on $n$ elements with no fixed points, no transpositions, and no 3-cycles is equal to the coefficient of $x^n$ in a generating function derived from a product over cycles of length $\geq 4$.

anchor_text: A probability space is separable if its $\sigma$-algebra has a countable generating class.
positive_text: A measure space is separable if there exists a countable family $\mathcal{C} \subset \mathcal{F}$ such that $\sigma(\mathcal{C}) = \mathcal{F}$.

negatives.text: Let $ \mathcal{A}_n $ be a nested sequence of $ \sigma $-algebras. If $ \int f d\mu_{\mathcal{A}_n} \to g $ in $ \mu $-a.e. sense, then $ g = \int f d\mu_{\mathcal{A}} $, where $ \mathcal{A} = \sigma(\cup_n \mathcal{A}_n) $.
The projection of a function $ f \in L^2(\mu) $ onto the subspace of $ \mathcal{A} $-measurable functions is the integral conditional to $ \mathcal{A} $.
The projection $ P_{\mathcal{G}} f $ of $ f \in L^2(\mu) $ onto the space of $ \mathcal{G} $-measurable functions is characterized as the closest $ \mathcal{G} $-measurable function in $ L^2 $.

anchor_text: The action of crystal operators on Schur functions can be described via skew Schur expansions, interpreting the crystal paths as shape deformations.
positive_text: Tableaux crystal operators act by shifting entries in semistandard Young tableaux, and this induces shape-based Schur coefficient changes.

negatives.text: A skew tableau can be transformed into a standard tableau shape via a sequence of moves that preserve the Schur function it represents.
Counting tableaux with weights on increasing shapes produces an exponential tableau generating function related to Gaussian integrals over shape parameters.
A generating function for skew tableaux is invariant under transposition if and only if the conjugate shape is the same.

anchor_text: In the category of finite sets, the cardinality of the domain of a morphism $f: A \to B$ equals the sum of the cardinalities of the fibers of $f$ over each element of $B$.
positive_text: If a function $f: A \to B$ has finite fibers, then $|A| = \sum_{b \in B} |f^{-1}(b)|$.

negatives.text: The inclusion map $i: A \to B$ is a morphism where $A \subseteq B$ and $i(a) = a$ for all $a \in A$.
The map $A \to A \times A$ sending $a \mapsto (a, a)$ is injective and its image is the diagonal subset of $A \times A$.
The image of a function $f: A \to B$ is the set $f[A]$, and this set can be obtained by quotienting $A$ by the equivalence relation $x \sim y$ if and only if $f(x) = f(y)$.

anchor_text: The composition of two epimorphisms in the category of modules over a field is an epimorphism.
positive_text: The composition of two surjective linear maps is surjective.

negatives.text: A vector space is projective if it is a direct summand of a free vector space.
Let $ V $ be a finite-dimensional vector space over $ \mathbb{F} $, and let $ T: V \to V $ be a linear transformation. The trace of $ T $ equals the trace of the induced map $ T^*: V^* \to V^* $.
The kernel of an endomorphism of a finite-dimensional vector space is the span of those basis vectors that map to zero.

anchor_text: The dimension of a vector space is the cardinality of any basis.
positive_text: The free rank of a free module is the cardinality of any basis.

negatives.text: Over a field, every module is torsion-free, meaning it has no non-zero elements with non-zero annihilators.
Two finitely generated free modules over a field are isomorphic precisely when they have equal free rank.
A set of module elements is linearly independent if and only if the corresponding module homomorphism is injective.

anchor_text: If the joint distribution of two random variables is absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure, then a joint probability density exists as the Radon–Nikodym derivative.\
positive_text: Suppose the pushforward of $\mu$ onto $\mathbb{R}^2$ is absolutely continuous with respect to the Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb{R}^2$; then the density exists by the Radon–Nikodym theorem.

negatives.text: A measure $ \nu $ is absolutely continuous with respect to the Lebesgue measure $ \lambda $ if there exists a non-negative $ f \in L^1 $ such that $ \nu(A) = \int_A f \, d\lambda $ for all Borel sets $ A $.
A measurable function is a mapping $f: \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ such that for every Borel set $B$, the preimage $f^{-1}(B)$ is in $\mathcal{F}$.
Let $ f \in L^1(\mu) $. The operator $ f \mapsto f_{\mathcal{F}} $ defines an idempotent linear operator on $ L^1 $ into itself.

anchor_text: Each Fourier mode of $ L^2(G) $ corresponds to an invariant Hilbert space, and the group action preserves the inner product on the space.
positive_text: Every irreducible representation of a compact group $ G $ is unitarizable, with an inner product invariant under the group action.

negatives.text: If the character of a finite-dimensional representation agrees with the character of an irreducible one on all group elements, then the two representations are isomorphic.
The Fourier transform of a function on a non-abelian group is a matrix-valued function on the set of irreducible representations.
The tensor product of two irreducible representations decomposes into a direct sum of irreducible representations.

anchor_text: A graph is ergodic if random walks on its vertices converge to a uniform stationary distribution.
positive_text: An irreducible matrix with a uniform positive eigenvector and dominant eigenvalue one implies asymptotic convergence to a uniform distribution under repeated application.

negatives.text: A minimal set of rows in the incidence matrix whose removal results in a matrix with a higher nullity corresponds to an edge cut.
A symmetric matrix is spectral arced if its eigenvalues are distributed in an arc-like curve when ordered by angular position.
A symmetric matrix has a non-identity permutation matrix that commutes with it if the system of equations is preserved under a permutation of coordinates.

anchor_text: Let $ f: A \to B $ be a function. Then the diagonal map $ \Delta_f: A \to A \times_B A $ defined by $ \Delta_f(x) = (x, x) $ is a coequalizer for the pair $ f \times f $ if and only if $ f $ is injective.
positive_text: Suppose $ f: A \to B $ is a morphism in the category of sets. The diagonal arrow $ \Delta: A \to A \times_B A $ is the coequalizer of the projections $ p_1, p_2: A \times A \to A $ precisely when $ f $ is monic.

negatives.text: A subobject of an object $B$ in $\mathbf{Set}$ is represented by a monomorphism $m: A \to B$, each representing the inclusion of a subset $A$ in $B$.

Given morphisms $f: A \to B$ and $g: B \to C$ in the category of sets, their composition $g \circ f: A \to C$ is the unique morphism satisfying the condition that for all $a \in A$, the image under $g \circ f$ is the same as the image of $f(a)$ under $g$.
Given morphisms $f : A \to B$ and $g : B \to C$, their composition yields a morphism $A \to C$ defined by the pasting of the diagram.

anchor_text: If $X$ is a real-valued random variable with distribution function $F$, then $F$ generates a probability measure on $\mathbb{R}$ via the Lebesgue–Stieltjes construction.
positive_text: If $F$ is a non-decreasing, right-continuous function on $\mathbb{R}$, then there exists a unique measure $\nu$ such that $\nu((a, b]) = F(b) - F(a)$ for all $a < b$.

negatives.text: If $(A_n)$ is a sequence of independent measurable sets in a probability space with $\sum \mu(A_n) = \infty$, then $\mu(\limsup A_n) = 1$.
The conditional measure $\mu(A \mid B)$ is defined as $\mu(A \cap B)/\mu(B)$ for $\mu(B) > 0$.

The covariance of two functions $ f $ and $ g $ on a measure space $ (S, \mathcal{F}, \mu) $ can be expressed as the integral of the conditional covariance given a sub-σ-algebra $ \mathcal{G} $ plus the covariance of the conditional integrals.

anchor_text: The image of a function $f : A \to B$ is the intersection of all subsets $C \subseteq B$ such that $f[A] \subseteq C$.
positive_text: The image of a morphism is the terminal subobject through which it factors.

negatives.text: In the category of sets, if a morphism $ f $ is a monomorphism, then it admits a retraction defined on the image of $ f $.

The equalizer of two morphisms $f, g: A \to B$ in the category of sets is the object $E$ equipped with a morphism $e: E \to A$ such that $f \circ e = g \circ e$, and it is universal with this property.
In **Set**, if two morphisms $f, g: A \to B$ are equalized by all maps from $A$ to any other object, then they are equal in the Hom-set Hom(A, B).

anchor_text: If $ f : X \to Y $ and $ g : Y \to Z $ are functions, and $ h = g \circ f $, then $ h^{-1} $ pulls back subsets via the images of $ f $ and $ g $ in composition order.
positive_text: In $ \mathbf{Set} $, the pullback of a composite morphism is expressible as the composition of the individual pullbacks.

negatives.text: In the category of sets, for any epimorphism $ f: X \to Y $, the kernel pair of $ f $ exists and the coequalizer of that pair is isomorphic to $ f $.
In the category **Set**, the identity morphism $1_A: A \to A$ is the unique morphism such that for any morphism $f: A \to B$, the composition $f \circ 1_A = f$.
In the category of sets, any morphism $ f: A \to B $ can be expressed as an epimorphism following a regular monomorphism.

anchor_text: A scheme $ X $ is generically reduced if its function field at each irreducible component is isomorphic to the function field of a reduced scheme.
positive_text: A scheme $ X = \mathrm{Spec}(A) $ is generically reduced if the localization of $ A $ at every minimal prime is reduced.

negatives.text: A ring homomorphism is finite if the codomain is finitely generated as a module over the domain.
A local ring is factorial if every height one prime ideal is principal.
A graded ring with a finitely generated homogeneous component in degree one determines a projective scheme.

anchor_text: A homomorphism of a finitely generated module is a central element if it commutes with all endomorphisms of the module.
positive_text: A linear transformation on a finite-dimensional vector space is central if it commutes with all elements of its endomorphism algebra.

negatives.text: The dual of a linear map sends the dual of the codomain into the dual of the domain and its kernel is the annihilator of the image.
The span of a quotient of a finite-dimensional vector space is determined by the images of a generating set under the canonical projection.
Every finite-dimensional vector space over a field is semisimple and can be written as a direct sum of one-dimensional subspaces.
